finding: One monarch, one composite style: 'DOM JOSEPH por graça de Deos Rey de Portugal e dos Algarves, d'áquem e d'além Mar, em Africa Senhor de Guiné...'. The style is used unchanged on acts of 1750, 1752, 1753, 1754, 1755 and 1756 in the same volume.
reading: A composite TITLE, not two crowns. The same style enumerates Guinea and India, which nobody proposes as separate territorial actors of this scenario.

finding: The Algarve title has been part of the Portuguese royal style continuously since the mid-13th century and remained so until 1910; there was never a separate Algarve succession, minority or regency.
reading: One crown wearing two titles is a titulature fact, not a personal union: a personal union needs two successions that can diverge.

finding: Every law is published through ONE Chancellaria mór da Corte e Reino and registered in ONE livro das Leys. Acts legislate for both in a single clause - 'nenhum dos Provedores, Deputados, e Officiaes da Companhia poderá nelles negociar em Portugal, ou nos Algarves' - rather than issuing a parallel Algarve act.
reading: Naples and Sicily each had their own chancery and their own parliament; a law for one was not a law for the other. Here one act binds both by naming both.

finding: The Algarve was divided in 1536 into two ORDINARY comarcas, Lagos and Tavira, each under a crown-appointed corregedor whose competences come from the Ordenações Manuelinas and Filipinas - the same magistracy, the same code, as every other comarca of Portugal. The Lei de 19 de Janeiro de 1756 regulates 'os Corregedores, e Ouvidores das Comarcas' as one body.
reading: A separate territorial actor does not receive its governors from the neighbour's magistracy under the neighbour's code.

finding: Appeals run to the Casa da Supplicação and the Relação do Porto, and supervision to the Mesa do Desembargo do Paço - the realm's own courts. No Algarve high court, no Algarve Council, no viceroy.
reading: This is the sharpest contrast with Naples and Sicily, each of which had its own supreme tribunals and its own viceroy.

finding: The Tavira corregedoria series holds royal treasury orders and décima records; the décima is the Portuguese crown's general tax. Customs clauses treat 'os Reinos de Portugal, e dos Algarves' as one fiscal space.
reading: One treasury, one tax, one customs regime.

finding: The Algarve had no Cortes of its own and the monarch was never sworn before an Algarve Cortes; it never had autonomous representation in the national arms. The cited study contrasts this directly with the Crown of Aragon, where the monarch had to be sworn before Cortes assembled in each constituent kingdom.
reading: The Aragonese test is the right one and the Algarve fails it.

finding: The study notes that 17th and 18th century FOREIGN cartographic representations of Iberia show two coats of arms for a crown that had only ever used one. The Le Rouge plate's ROYAUME DE ALGARVE lettering is an instance of that convention.
reading: The very evidence MAPGEN-026 withheld on is identified in the literature as a foreign engraving habit. It is not actor evidence, in either direction.
